Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$
([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]), let $x\in D$, and let
$p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Define the open parameter set $S_{x,p}:=\{t\in\mathbb R:x+tp\in D\}$,
which contains $0$, the feasible ray $T_{x,p}:=S_{x,p}\cap[0,\infty)$,
and $\phi(t):=f(x+tp)$ for $t\in S_{x,p}$. At every $t\in S_{x,p}$,
including $0$, the chain rule gives $\phi'(t)=Df(x+tp)p$.
By [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
the matrix of $Df$ is the Jacobian, whose scalar-field row is the transpose
of the gradient. Hence
$\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$, using the gradient convention
of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A direction is a **descent direction** at
$x$ when $\phi'(0)=\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle<0$.

Assume for the line-search conditions below that $p$ is a descent direction
at $x$.
Fix constants $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$. A feasible step $t>0$ is a **Wolfe step**
when
$$
\phi(t)\le\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0),\qquad \phi'(t)\ge c_2\phi'(0).
$$
It is a **strong Wolfe step** when it satisfies the first inequality and
$$
|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|.
$$
The first inequality is the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition. The second
Wolfe inequality is the curvature condition. Every strong Wolfe step is a
Wolfe step, because $\phi'(0)<0$ and the strong curvature bound implies
$\phi'(t)\ge-c_2|\phi'(0)|=c_2\phi'(0)$.

For a descent direction define its **descent angle** $\theta\in[0,\pi/2)$ by
$$
\cos\theta:=-\frac{\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle}{\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\|p\|_2}.
$$
The denominator is nonzero for a descent direction. The Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] ensures $0<\cos\theta\le1$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

derivations.claim: The chain rule in [F1] makes $\phi$ continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of each finite point of $[0,\infty)$. Define $\psi(t):=\phi(t)-\phi(0)-c_1t\phi'(0)$. Then $\psi(0)=0$ and $d:=\psi'(0)=(1-c_1)\phi'(0)<0$. By [F3], $\psi(t)/t\to d$ as $t\to0$. Choose $\delta>0$ so that $\psi(t)/t<d/2<0$ for $0<t<\delta$; hence $\psi(t)<0$ there.

Since $\phi$ is bounded below and $-c_1\phi'(0)>0$, $\psi(t)\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$. Thus $S:=\{t>0:\psi(t)\ge0\}$ is nonempty and bounded away from $0$. Let $t_*:=\inf S>0$. Continuity of $\psi$ implies $\psi(t_*)=0$: values below $t_*$ have $\psi<0$, while a sequence of points of $S$ converges to $t_*$.

Every $s\in(0,t_*)$ has $\psi(s)<0$, so Armijo holds strictly throughout that interval. Apply [F2] to $\phi$ on $[0,t_*]$ to get $\xi\in(0,t_*)$ with $\phi'(\xi)=(\phi(t_*)-\phi(0))/t_*=c_1\phi'(0)$. Hence $|\phi'(\xi)|=c_1|\phi'(0)|<c_2|\phi'(0)|$, so the strong curvature inequality holds strictly at $\xi$.

The strict Armijo inequality holds at every point of $(0,t_*)$, including $\xi$, and both $\phi$ and $\phi'$ are continuous there. Therefore both strict inequalities persist on some open interval about $\xi$ contained in $(0,t_*)$. Every point of that interval is a strong Wolfe step, proving the asserted nonemptiness.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

$$
\|\nabla f(u)-\nabla f(v)\|_2\le L\|u-v\|_2\qquad(u,v\in N).
$$
For every $k\ge0$, assume $x_{k+1}=x_k+t_kp_k$, $p_k\ne0$ is a descent
direction at $x_k$, and $t_k>0$ is a Wolfe step for $f,x_k,p_k$ under

$$\cos\theta_k:=-\frac{\langle\nabla f(x_k),p_k\rangle}{\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2\|p_k\|_2}.$$
Then
$$
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\cos^2\theta_k\,\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2^2<\infty.
$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  Suppose $A:=Df(a)$ is invertible and put
$B:=A^{-1}$.  Then there are $R>0$, $0\le q<1$, and $C>0$ such that
$\overline B(a,R)\subseteq U$, $\|Bv\|_2\le C\|v\|_2$, and, for every
$y\in\mathbb R^n$, the Newton map

$$T_y(x):=x+B(y-f(x))$$

satisfies

$$\|T_y(x)-T_y(z)\|_2\le q\|x-z\|_2\qquad(x,z\in\overline B(a,R)).$$

Moreover $Df(x)$ is invertible for every $x\in\overline B(a,R)$ and

$$\|Df(x)^{-1}v\|_2\le\frac C{1-q}\|v\|_2.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and write $J(x)=DF(x)$ as a matrix in the standard basis. The matrix
of $DF(x)$ agrees with the Jacobian matrix by
[[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For a
matrix $A$ let
$\|A\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$. Let $K\subseteq U$ be convex,
let $x_*,x\in K$, and suppose for some $L\ge0$ that
$$\|J(y)-J(z)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|y-z\|_2\qquad(y,z\in K).$$
Then
$$\|F(x)-F(x_*)-J(x)(x-x_*)\|_2\le\frac{L}{2}\|x-x_*\|_2^2.$$

Let $n\ge1$.  A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$
([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$B(Au)=u\quad\hbox{and}\quad A(Bu)=u\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n).$$

The map $B$ is unique: if $C$ has the same two properties, then
$C=C\circ(A\circ B)=(C\circ A)\circ B=B$.  It is denoted $A^{-1}$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Every claimed estimate is $0\le0$, so the assertion holds. For the remainder assume $n\ge1$, so the imported positive-dimensional Newton lemmas and operator-norm comparisons apply.

$x_*\in U$ satisfy $F(x_*)=0$ with $J_*:=DF(x_*)$ invertible. Suppose a
closed Euclidean ball $K=\overline B_2(x_*,R)\subseteq U$ with $R>0$ is convex and
$$
\|J(u)-J(v)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|u-v\|_2\qquad(u,v\in K),
$$
where $J(x):=DF(x)$ and
$\|A\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$ for $n\ge1$;
for $n=0$ set the norm of the unique linear map to $0$. Let
$\|v\|_*:=\|J_*v\|_2$ and fix $\bar\eta\in[0,1)$. There are constants
$r_0>0$, $C_F>0$, and $C\ge0$ such that, whenever
$\|x-x_*\|_2\le r_0$, $0\le\eta\le\bar\eta$, and $p,r\in\mathbb R^n$
satisfy
$$
J(x)p+F(x)=r,\qquad \|r\|_2\le\eta\|F(x)\|_2,
$$
then $J(x)$ is invertible,
$\|F(x)\|_2\le C_F\|x-x_*\|_*$, and
$$
\|x+p-x_*\|_*\le\bigl(\eta+C\|x-x_*\|_*\bigr)\|x-x_*\|_*.
$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.
Let $k\ge2$. If $f\in C^k(U)$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, then every iterated derivative of $f$ of order $k$ is unchanged by any permutation of its coordinate differentiations.

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, every iterate, residual and correction is the unique zero vector and $x_k=x_*$ for all $k$. Choose any $\rho>0$ and $q=(1+\bar\eta)/2<1$; all error bounds are $0\le0$. The exact-root alternative applies from the start, including the quadratic zero-error bound. For the remainder assume $n\ge1$.
Let $C_F,C$ and a radius $r_0$ be supplied by [F1], and let $K_*:=\|J_*^{-1}\|_{\rm op}$. Set $q:=(1+\bar\eta)/2<1$. Choose $\rho>0$ with $K_*\rho\le r_0$ and, when $C>0$, $C\rho\le(1-\bar\eta)/2$.

Suppose $\|x_k-x_*\|_*\le\rho$. Then $\|x_k-x_*\|_2\le K_*\rho\le r_0$, so [F1] applies and gives $\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_*\le(\eta_k+C\|x_k-x_*\|_*)\|x_k-x_*\|_*\le q\|x_k-x_*\|_*\le\rho$. Induction proves every iterate remains in the ball and the geometric bound.

By [F2] and step 2.1, $\|x_k-x_*\|_*\to0$. If $x_k\ne x_*$, divide the recurrence in [F1] by $\|x_k-x_*\|_*$ to get $\frac{\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_*}{\|x_k-x_*\|_*}\le\eta_k+C\|x_k-x_*\|_*$. When $\eta_k\to0$, the right side tends to zero. If some $x_k=x_*$, then $F(x_k)=0$ and the residual bound gives $r_k=0$; local invertibility in [F1] forces $p_k=0$, so all later iterates remain there.
If $\eta_k\le C_\eta\|F(x_k)\|_2$, [F1] and step 2.1 yield $\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_*\le\bigl(C_\eta C_F+C\bigr)\|x_k-x_*\|_*^2$, which is quadratic convergence in the $*$ norm.

In the specialization $F=\nabla f$ with $f\in C^2(U)$, each $F_i=\partial_i f$ has continuous first partials. By [F5] it is totally differentiable, and by [F4] the matrix of $DF$ has entries $J_{ij}=\partial_j(\partial_i f)$. By [F6] these equal $\partial_i(\partial_j f)$, the entries of the Hessian in [F3]. Thus $J(x)=\nabla^2f(x)$. Invertibility gives $K_*^{-1}\|e\|_2\le\|e\|_*\le\|J_*\|_{\rm op}\|e\|_2$ for every $e$. These fixed comparison constants transfer the linear, superlinear, and quadratic bounds from the $*$ norm to the Euclidean norm. The fixed-$\bar\eta$ geometric estimate of step 2.1 is linear convergence.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be twice continuously differentiable, meaning that $f$ is $C^1$ and its
gradient is $C^1$.
Write $g(x):=\nabla f(x)$ and $H(x):=\nabla^2f(x)$ using
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. The identity matrix $I_n$ and
matrix-vector products have the convention of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Use the matrix-free access
model of [[def-matrix-free-access-model-for-krylov-methods]] for products
$v\mapsto(H(x)+\lambda I_n)v$.

**Linear-solver input:** a fixed deterministic Krylov procedure $K$ which accepts a
matrix-free linear operator $A$, a right-hand side $b$, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$,
and a finite inner-iteration budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$. It returns either
`no-candidate` or `candidate` with a vector $p$ and an iteration count
$m\in\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$ satisfying $p\in K_m(A,b)$, where $K_m$ is as defined
by [[def-krylov-subspace-of-a-matrix-and-start-vector]]. A candidate's residual
status is never trusted: this algorithm recomputes
the requested residual using the supplied operator. **Other inputs:** $x_0\in U$, outer update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$, forcing values $\eta_k\in[0,\bar\eta]$ for a fixed
$0\le\bar\eta<1$, descent parameter $\sigma\in(0,1)$, regularization factor
$\gamma>1$, initial shift $\lambda_0>0$, shift cap $\lambda_{\max}\ge\lambda_0$,
regularized-attempt budget $J\in\mathbb N_0$, inner budget $M$, and the
parameters and finite expansion/zoom budgets of
[[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]]. **Output:** the last valid
iterate and one of `stationary`, `iteration-budget-exhausted`,
`no-descent-direction`, or `line-search-failure`; in the last case also
return the underlying line-search failure cause.

At iteration $k=0,1,\ldots,N$:

1. Compute $g_k:=g(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
   If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted})$.
2. Set $\lambda:=0$. For $j=0,1,\ldots,J$, call $K$ on
   $A_\lambda v:=H(x_k)v+\lambda I_nv$, right-hand side $-g_k$, tolerance
   $\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$, and budget $M$. A `no-candidate` result is a rejected
   attempt. If it returns a candidate $p$, compute
   $r:=(H(x_k)+\lambda I_n)p+g_k$. Accept this linear solve only when
   $\|r\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$ and
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$; otherwise reject it.
   If the attempt is rejected and either $j=J$ or $\lambda=\lambda_{\max}$, stop the
   regularization loop. Otherwise set
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\lambda_0\}$ when $\lambda=0$, and
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\gamma\lambda\}$ when $\lambda>0$;
   then continue with the next $j$.
3. If no regularized attempt was accepted, set $p:=-g_k$ and check
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$. If this check fails,
   return `no-descent-direction`. For the stated $\sigma$ and $g_k\ne0$ it
   passes, but the check remains part of the procedure.
4. Call [[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]] at $x_k$ in direction $p$.
   If it returns failure, return $(x_k,\texttt{line-search-failure},s)$, where $s$ is
   the returned line-search failure cause. Otherwise, for its returned strong Wolfe step $t_k$,
   set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t_kp$ and continue.

The first unregularized system uses the forcing residual
$\|H(x_k)p+g_k\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$. A regularized attempt checks the
residual for the shifted system instead. Finite inner, regularization, and
line-search budgets can return failure; the procedure makes no global
convergence claim. The local rate theorem applies only to an unshifted
$\lambda=0$ sequence taking full steps $t_k=1$ and remaining in its stated
local tube. This algorithm does not assert that every run enters that branch.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$,
let $x\in D$, and let $p\in\mathbb R^n$ be arbitrary. Fix $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$ and finite
budgets $E,Z\in\mathbb N$ for expansion and zoom trials. After the direction check passes, use the functions
$\phi(t)=f(x+tp)$ and $\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$ from
[[def-wolfe-and-strong-wolfe-conditions]]. **Output:** either a positive
strong Wolfe step, or one of `invalid-direction`, `domain-exit`, and
`evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

1. If $\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle\ge0$, return `invalid-direction`.
   Set $a:=0$ and $t:=1$. For at most $E$ expansion trials, in order:
   - If $x+tp\notin D$, return `domain-exit` without evaluating the trial.
   - Evaluate $\phi(t)$ and $\phi'(t)$. If
     $\phi(t)>\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0)$ or $\phi(t)\ge\phi(a)$, call the zoom
     procedure below with the ordered endpoint pair $(a,t)$ and return its
     output.
   - If $|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|$, return $t$ as a strong Wolfe step.
   - If $\phi'(t)\ge0$, call zoom with the reversed endpoint pair $(t,a)$ and
     return its output.
   - Otherwise set $a:=t$ and $t:=2t$.
2. If the expansion budget is exhausted, return `evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

For `zoom(a,b)`, preserve the endpoint order even when $b<a$. For at most
$Z$ zoom trials, in order:

1. Set $m:=(a+b)/2$. If $x+mp\notin D$, return `domain-exit` without
   evaluating the trial.
2. Evaluate $\phi(m)$ and $\phi'(m)$. If
   $\phi(m)>\phi(0)+c_1m\phi'(0)$ or $\phi(m)\ge\phi(a)$, set $b:=m$.
   Otherwise, if $|\phi'(m)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|$, return $m$ as a strong Wolfe
   step. In the remaining branch, if $\phi'(m)(b-a)\ge0$, first set
   $b:=a$; then set $a:=m$.
3. If the zoom budget is exhausted, return `evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

The procedure returns a step only after both strong Wolfe inequalities have
been checked. Finite budgets and domain exits may return failure even when a
strong Wolfe step exists; no convergence claim follows from the procedure
alone.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$
([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]), let $x\in D$, and let
$p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Define the open parameter set $S_{x,p}:=\{t\in\mathbb R:x+tp\in D\}$,
which contains $0$, the feasible ray $T_{x,p}:=S_{x,p}\cap[0,\infty)$,
and $\phi(t):=f(x+tp)$ for $t\in S_{x,p}$. At every $t\in S_{x,p}$,
including $0$, the chain rule gives $\phi'(t)=Df(x+tp)p$.
By [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
the matrix of $Df$ is the Jacobian, whose scalar-field row is the transpose
of the gradient. Hence
$\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$, using the gradient convention
of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A direction is a **descent direction** at
$x$ when $\phi'(0)=\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle<0$.

Assume for the line-search conditions below that $p$ is a descent direction
at $x$.
Fix constants $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$. A feasible step $t>0$ is a **Wolfe step**
when
$$
\phi(t)\le\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0),\qquad \phi'(t)\ge c_2\phi'(0).
$$
It is a **strong Wolfe step** when it satisfies the first inequality and
$$
|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|.
$$
The first inequality is the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition. The second
Wolfe inequality is the curvature condition. Every strong Wolfe step is a
Wolfe step, because $\phi'(0)<0$ and the strong curvature bound implies
$\phi'(t)\ge-c_2|\phi'(0)|=c_2\phi'(0)$.

For a descent direction define its **descent angle** $\theta\in[0,\pi/2)$ by
$$
\cos\theta:=-\frac{\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle}{\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\|p\|_2}.
$$
The denominator is nonzero for a descent direction. The Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] ensures $0<\cos\theta\le1$.

$p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Define the open parameter set $S_{x,p}:=\{t\in\mathbb R:x+tp\in D\}$,
which contains $0$, the feasible ray $T_{x,p}:=S_{x,p}\cap[0,\infty)$,
and $\phi(t):=f(x+tp)$ for $t\in S_{x,p}$. At every $t\in S_{x,p}$,
including $0$, the chain rule gives $\phi'(t)=Df(x+tp)p$.
By [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
the matrix of $Df$ is the Jacobian, whose scalar-field row is the transpose
of the gradient. Hence
$\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$, using the gradient convention
of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A direction is a **descent direction** at
$x$ when $\phi'(0)=\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle<0$.

Assume for the line-search conditions below that $p$ is a descent direction
at $x$.
Fix constants $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$. A feasible step $t>0$ is a **Wolfe step**
when
$$
\phi(t)\le\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0),\qquad \phi'(t)\ge c_2\phi'(0).
$$
It is a **strong Wolfe step** when it satisfies the first inequality and
$$
|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|.
$$
The first inequality is the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition. The second
Wolfe inequality is the curvature condition. Every strong Wolfe step is a
Wolfe step, because $\phi'(0)<0$ and the strong curvature bound implies
$\phi'(t)\ge-c_2|\phi'(0)|=c_2\phi'(0)$.

For a descent direction define its **descent angle** $\theta\in[0,\pi/2)$ by
$$
\cos\theta:=-\frac{\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle}{\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\|p\|_2}.
$$
The denominator is nonzero for a descent direction. The Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] ensures $0<\cos\theta\le1$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be twice continuously differentiable, meaning that $f$ is $C^1$ and its
gradient is $C^1$.
Write $g(x):=\nabla f(x)$ and $H(x):=\nabla^2f(x)$ using
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. The identity matrix $I_n$ and
matrix-vector products have the convention of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Use the matrix-free access
model of [[def-matrix-free-access-model-for-krylov-methods]] for products
$v\mapsto(H(x)+\lambda I_n)v$.

**Linear-solver input:** a fixed deterministic Krylov procedure $K$ which accepts a
matrix-free linear operator $A$, a right-hand side $b$, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$,
and a finite inner-iteration budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$. It returns either
`no-candidate` or `candidate` with a vector $p$ and an iteration count
$m\in\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$ satisfying $p\in K_m(A,b)$, where $K_m$ is as defined
by [[def-krylov-subspace-of-a-matrix-and-start-vector]]. A candidate's residual
status is never trusted: this algorithm recomputes
the requested residual using the supplied operator. **Other inputs:** $x_0\in U$, outer update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$, forcing values $\eta_k\in[0,\bar\eta]$ for a fixed
$0\le\bar\eta<1$, descent parameter $\sigma\in(0,1)$, regularization factor
$\gamma>1$, initial shift $\lambda_0>0$, shift cap $\lambda_{\max}\ge\lambda_0$,
regularized-attempt budget $J\in\mathbb N_0$, inner budget $M$, and the
parameters and finite expansion/zoom budgets of
[[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]]. **Output:** the last valid
iterate and one of `stationary`, `iteration-budget-exhausted`,
`no-descent-direction`, or `line-search-failure`; in the last case also
return the underlying line-search failure cause.

At iteration $k=0,1,\ldots,N$:

1. Compute $g_k:=g(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
   If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted})$.
2. Set $\lambda:=0$. For $j=0,1,\ldots,J$, call $K$ on
   $A_\lambda v:=H(x_k)v+\lambda I_nv$, right-hand side $-g_k$, tolerance
   $\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$, and budget $M$. A `no-candidate` result is a rejected
   attempt. If it returns a candidate $p$, compute
   $r:=(H(x_k)+\lambda I_n)p+g_k$. Accept this linear solve only when
   $\|r\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$ and
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$; otherwise reject it.
   If the attempt is rejected and either $j=J$ or $\lambda=\lambda_{\max}$, stop the
   regularization loop. Otherwise set
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\lambda_0\}$ when $\lambda=0$, and
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\gamma\lambda\}$ when $\lambda>0$;
   then continue with the next $j$.
3. If no regularized attempt was accepted, set $p:=-g_k$ and check
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$. If this check fails,
   return `no-descent-direction`. For the stated $\sigma$ and $g_k\ne0$ it
   passes, but the check remains part of the procedure.
4. Call [[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]] at $x_k$ in direction $p$.
   If it returns failure, return $(x_k,\texttt{line-search-failure},s)$, where $s$ is
   the returned line-search failure cause. Otherwise, for its returned strong Wolfe step $t_k$,
   set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t_kp$ and continue.

The first unregularized system uses the forcing residual
$\|H(x_k)p+g_k\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$. A regularized attempt checks the
residual for the shifted system instead. Finite inner, regularization, and
line-search budgets can return failure; the procedure makes no global
convergence claim. The local rate theorem applies only to an unshifted
$\lambda=0$ sequence taking full steps $t_k=1$ and remaining in its stated
local tube. This algorithm does not assert that every run enters that branch.

Under the inputs of [[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]], assume all requested in-domain function and gradient evaluations terminate with real values and all prescribed comparisons are exact. The procedure terminates with its specified step or failure status. It makes at most $E$ expansion trial evaluations and at most one zoom call with at most $Z$ trial evaluations, hence at most $E+Z$ evaluated trial points. Each evaluates the objective and directional derivative at that point. Every returned step is positive, feasible, and satisfies both strong Wolfe inequalities. A domain-exit trial is not evaluated. The bound excludes the initial-point data and does not bound arithmetic work or guarantee success when a strong Wolfe step exists.

derivations.claim: Initially $x_0\in U$. At any nonstationary iteration the supplied solver calls and candidate residual evaluations terminate by assumption; the loop has at most $J+1$ attempts. Every accepted candidate satisfies $g_k^Tp<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2<0$, since a candidate with $p=0$ cannot pass. If none passes, $p=-g_k$ gives $g_k^Tp=-\|g_k\|_2^2<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2^2$ because $g_k\ne0$ and $0<\sigma<1$. Thus a strict descent direction is always available and the fallback failure cannot occur in exact arithmetic.

By [F2] the ensuing search terminates. On failure the algorithm returns its last valid iterate, its line-search-failure status and the search cause. On success feasibility of the checked step gives $x_{k+1}\in U$. Induction proves feasibility of every iterate.

A solve or update can occur only for $k<N$. Thus at most $N$ updates and searches and $N(J+1)$ solver calls occur; each uses at most $M$ inner iterations. At most one candidate residual is recomputed per call, each by one Hessian action plus the displayed shift and vector arithmetic. By [F2] there are at most $N(E+Z)$ evaluated search trials. The outer loop computes its gradient once per visited index, at most $N+1$ times, separately from line-search gradient evaluations.

Every inner call and search terminates and every loop has its finite stated bound. Hence the algorithm reaches a specified return no later than its $k=N$ check. Steps 1.1–3.1 prove the asserted statuses, feasibility and counts; they do not specify the internal Hessian-action count of the arbitrary solver or a convergence theorem.
